extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers or fans interested in comedy history and performance
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biographical article about Imogene Coca describing her life, career, signature techniques, roles, and recognition as an American comic actress from vaudeville to late-life television and stage work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial expressiveness / 'rubbery' face
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessed a 'rubbery' face capable of the broadest expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life magazine compared her to Beatrice Lillie and Charlie Chaplin and described her characterizations as taking 'people or situations suspended in their own precarious balance between dignity and absurdity, and push(ing) them over the cliff with one single, pointed gesture.' Use of exaggerated, highly readable facial expression is presented as a core comedic instrument in her work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety and light touch in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: A quieter, delicate approach to satire rather than brash, noisy, 'sledge-hammer' methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life noted that unlike many satirists who are 'brash, noisy, and indelicate' and 'use a sledge hammer to smash a butterfly,' Coca was 'the timid woman who, when aroused, can beat a tiger to death with a feather.' The page treats understated, precise gestures and restraint as an effective comedic strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blending music/dance with comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining musical and dance skills with comedic performance as a defining mode of her act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: She began as a dancer and musician and 'gained prominence when she combined music with comedy.' Example: her comic striptease routine (making sultry faces and gestures but removing only one glove) and early film shorts like The Bashful Ballerina and Dime a Dance illustrate how musicality was integrated into comedic timing and gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical parody and dance-based sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: Using dance and parody (e.g., of classic ballets) as material for comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Your Show of Shows she frequently starred in parodies of classic ballets (often opposite dancer/choreographer James Starbuck), demonstrating that skilled physical performance and choreography could be repurposed for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring stock characters and socially conscious pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating recurring stock characters that blend humor with pathos and social awareness (e.g., the 'bag lady').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One early stock character blended comedy with socially conscious pathos as a bag lady; she was frequently asked to reprise the role. The article presents this as a method for building memorable, repeatable comedic personas that resonate emotionally as well as comically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility across media and genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to perform across vaudeville, cabaret, film, theater, television, voice work, and music videos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coca worked in stage musical revues, television sketch comedy, sitcoms, films, voice roles in children's programs, and even an MTV music video. The page implicitly treats cross-media adaptability as evidence of comedic skill and career resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career adaptability and reinvention
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinvention at different career stages (e.g., transitioning to celebrated television comedian in her 40s, returning to Broadway at 70).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes she graduated from dance/music into decades of stage revues and in her 40s began a celebrated television comedy career; later she returned to Broadway with a Tony-nominated performance at age 70. Adaptability and successful role-reinvention are presented as hallmarks of her longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical skills and acrobatic background informing comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Early training as a child acrobat, ballet and dance lessons contributed to physical comedy ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting out in vaudeville as a child acrobat and studying ballet are cited as foundations for her physicality on stage and in parodic dance sketches; physical training is framed as a resource for comedic performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and strong work ethic
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrated professional dedication and endurance under difficult working conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 1999 interview anecdote recounts Coca sitting for hours in 15°F snow during an MTV shoot without complaint, with the producer calling her 'the most professional artist I've ever worked with.' The page treats unwavering professionalism as a respected attribute for performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical recognition and awards as indicators of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Emmy wins/nominations, Peabody Award, Tony nomination and other honors as measures of achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coca was nominated for five Emmys for Your Show of Shows (winning Best Actress in 1951), received a Peabody Award (1953), a Tony nomination (1978), and a sixth Emmy nomination at age 80. The article uses such honors to evidence the quality and impact of her work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to create memorable guest and supporting roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Making lasting impressions through guest appearances and supporting parts in sitcoms, specials, and films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Her numerous guest appearances (e.g., Bewitched, The Brady Bunch, Moonlighting) and character roles like 'Aunt Edna' in National Lampoon's Vacation are presented as part of a body of work that sustained visibility and influence, showing that strong character work outside starring roles can define a career.
